lead: The skipper makes the weather decisions, but the whole crew lives with them. Know how wind is named and measured, what a forecast is telling you, and which signs in the sky and on the barometer deserve a word to the skipper.

sections.title: Named by where it comes from

qa.q: Does a northerly wind blow from the north or towards the north?
qa.a: From the north: **wind direction** is always named after where the wind blows from. A flag streams downwind, so one streaming towards the south-east shows a north-westerly.

blocks.p: Wind is always named after the direction it blows **from**. A northerly blows from the north towards the south; a sea breeze blows in from the sea.

fig.note: A northerly: from the north, pushing you south

blocks.p: Flags, smoke and boats at anchor show the wind the other way round: a flag streams **downwind**. If it streams towards the south-east, the wind is a north-westerly.

qa.q: How many knots is Force 5 on the Beaufort scale?
qa.a: 17 to 21 knots, a fresh breeze with many white horses: time to reef. On the **Beaufort scale** Force 4 is 11–16 knots, Force 6 is 22–27, and Force 8, a gale, is 34–40.

blocks.p: Forecasts give the wind as a **Force** on the Beaufort scale. Each Force is a band of wind speeds in knots, and the sea grows with it.

blocks.label: Remember

qa.q: What does "N 3 to 4, increasing 5 later" mean in a sailing forecast?
qa.a: A northerly Force 3 to 4 now, building to Force 5 later in the day: words of change such as **increasing**, becoming and later describe the rest of the day, not just the morning.

blocks.p: A marine forecast keeps to one order: wind direction and Force, the state of the sea, the weather, the visibility. Listen for the words of change: **increasing**, **becoming**, **later**. They describe the rest of the day, not just the morning.

sections.title: The daily wind of a hot coast

qa.q: What time does the sea breeze start, and when does it die?
qa.a: Around midday: on a hot, settled day the **sea breeze** fills in about noon, is strongest in mid-afternoon and dies at sunset. At night a light land breeze drifts offshore until morning.

blocks.p: On a hot, settled day the land heats up faster than the sea. Warm air rises over the land and cooler air flows in from the sea to replace it: the **sea breeze**. It fills in around midday, is strongest in mid-afternoon and dies at sunset.

A calm morning anchorage close off a beach can have the wind blowing onto that beach by three o'clock. At night it reverses: the land cools faster than the sea, and a light **land breeze** drifts offshore until morning.

sections.title: Where the land makes the wind

qa.q: What time of day is the Meltemi strongest in the Aegean?
qa.a: In the afternoon: the **Meltemi**, the Aegean's summer northerly, often blows Force 5 to 7 for days, usually eases overnight and builds through the day. That is why crews in the Cyclades sail early.

blocks.p: The **Meltemi** is the summer wind of the Aegean. It blows from the north under clear skies, often Force 5 to 7 for days on end. It usually eases overnight and builds through the day to its strongest in the afternoon. So crews in the Cyclades make their passages early, and any leg towards the north is a beat into wind and waves.

tiles.name: A gap between islands
tiles.note: the wind is squeezed: stronger at A

blocks.p: Land bends any wind and speeds it up. It **funnels** through gaps between islands and round headlands, where it blows harder than in open water. In the lee of high land the water may look calm, but the wind that has climbed over the top falls down the slope in sudden, violent gusts.

qa.q: How fast does the barometer have to fall to warn of strong wind?
qa.a: A fall of several hPa in three hours warns of strong wind: on the **barometer** the change matters more than the number. Steady or slowly rising pressure means settled weather.

blocks.p: The **barometer** shows air pressure in hectopascals (hPa). The number itself matters less than the change, which is why it is logged every few hours. Steady or slowly rising pressure means settled weather. A fall of several hPa in three hours warns of strong wind.

lines: Down 3 hPa, then 6 hPa in three hours

blocks.p: Put the signs together. Pressure falling fast, high wispy cloud thickening from the west and a long swell arriving out of a calm sea all say the same thing: a **depression** with strong wind is on its way.

sections.title: Reef before the squall, not in it

qa.q: What should we do when a thunderstorm squall is coming?
qa.a: Reef or drop the sails, put lifejackets on, shut the hatches and stow loose gear before the **squall** arrives: its first gust can be far stronger than the wind ahead of it and comes within minutes.

blocks.p: On a hot, sticky afternoon watch the tall cauliflower clouds that grow over the land. When a top spreads out flat like an anvil, it is a thundercloud. Under it comes a **squall**: sudden violent gusts, often from a new direction, heavy rain and lightning.

fig.title: Before the squall arrives
lines: Reef or drop the sails now
Watch the dark line on the water

blocks.p: The first gust can be far stronger than the wind ahead of it, and it reaches you within minutes of the dark ruffled water appearing. Everything is easier to do before it arrives.
